flashcards.question: What is the difference between TRAVEL and TOURISM?
flashcards.answer:
TRAVEL = the activity of travellers; a TRAVELLER is anyone moving between geographic locations for ANY purpose and ANY duration.

TOURISM = the activity of VISITORS. Tourism is therefore a SUBSET of travel, and visitors are a subset of travellers.
flashcards.explanation: Key framing from the UN International Recommendations for Tourism Statistics (2008).

flashcards.question: What is a VISITOR, and how is a TOURIST different from an EXCURSIONIST?
flashcards.answer:
A VISITOR is a traveller taking a trip to a main destination OUTSIDE their usual environment, for LESS THAN A YEAR, for any purpose other than being employed by a resident entity there.

• TOURIST (overnight visitor) = the trip INCLUDES an overnight stay
• SAME-DAY VISITOR / EXCURSIONIST = no overnight stay
flashcards.explanation: Overnight stay is the dividing line between tourist and excursionist.

flashcards.question: What are the 3 BASIC FORMS of tourism (by country of reference)?
flashcards.answer:
1. DOMESTIC tourism — resident visitor WITHIN the country of reference
2. INBOUND tourism — NON-resident visitor within the country of reference
3. OUTBOUND tourism — resident visitor OUTSIDE the country of reference
flashcards.explanation: Defined relative to the 'country of reference'.

flashcards.question: How do the 3 basic forms combine into INTERNAL, NATIONAL and INTERNATIONAL tourism?
flashcards.answer:
• INTERNAL = DOMESTIC + INBOUND (all activity within the country)
• NATIONAL = DOMESTIC + OUTBOUND (all activity of residents)
• INTERNATIONAL = INBOUND + OUTBOUND (all cross-border activity)
flashcards.explanation: Three derived forms built from the three basic ones.

flashcards.question: What is a TOURISM DESTINATION (UN Tourism)?
flashcards.answer:
A PHYSICAL SPACE (with or without administrative boundaries) in which a visitor can spend an OVERNIGHT.

It is the cluster (co-location) of products, services, activities and experiences along the tourism value chain, and the basic unit of analysis of tourism. It is also intangible — its IMAGE and IDENTITY influence its market competitiveness.
flashcards.explanation: A destination can be a country, region, island, town or a self-contained centre.

flashcards.question: What is SUSTAINABLE TOURISM?
flashcards.answer: "Tourism that takes full account of its current and future ECONOMIC, SOCIAL and ENVIRONMENTAL impacts, addressing the needs of visitors, the industry, the environment and host communities" (UNWTO, 2005).
flashcards.explanation: The three pillars: economic, social, environmental.

flashcards.question: What is a TOURISM PRODUCT?
flashcards.answer:
A combination of TANGIBLE and INTANGIBLE elements — natural, cultural and man-made resources, attractions, facilities, services and activities — around a specific centre of interest.

It is the core of the destination marketing mix, creates an overall visitor experience, is priced and sold through distribution channels, and has a LIFE-CYCLE.
flashcards.explanation: Tangible + intangible around a 'centre of interest'.

flashcards.question: How many SDGs are there, and how does tourism relate to them?
flashcards.answer:
There are 17 interrelated Sustainable Development Goals (169 targets, 231 indicators).

The 'SDGs Wedding Cake' shows three pillars: ENVIRONMENT (biosphere) as the base, SOCIETY as the middle layer, ECONOMY at the top. Well-managed tourism can advance all 17 SDGs when sustainability is a shared responsibility.
flashcards.explanation: 17 SDGs; tourism cuts across the environment–society–economy pillars.

flashcards.question: What is the TOURISM VALUE CHAIN?
flashcards.answer:
The sequence of PRIMARY and SUPPORT activities strategically fundamental to the tourism sector's performance.

• PRIMARY: policy & planning, product development & packaging, promotion & marketing, distribution & sales, destination operations & services
• SUPPORT: transport & infrastructure, HR development, technology & systems, complementary goods/services
flashcards.explanation: Used to trace income flow and find collaborative value.

learn.title: Introduction to Tourism and Sustainability
learn.content:
Key Definitions (UN, 2010)

TRAVEL = activity of travellers (any purpose, any duration)
TOURISM = activity of VISITORS → a subset of travel
TOURIST = overnight visitor · EXCURSIONIST = same-day visitor

Forms of Tourism

  • Basic: Domestic · Inbound · Outbound
  • Derived: Internal (D+I) · National (D+O) · International (I+O)

Destination & Product

A tourism destination is a physical space where a visitor can spend an overnight — a cluster of products and experiences whose image/identity drives competitiveness. A tourism product combines tangible + intangible elements and has a life-cycle.

Sustainability & SDGs

Sustainable tourism balances economic, social and environmental impacts. The 17 SDGs ('Wedding Cake': environment → society → economy) can all be advanced by well-managed tourism.

Tourism Value Chain

Primary activities (policy, product, marketing, distribution, operations) + support activities (transport, HR, technology) — used to trace income and create collaborative value.

flashcards.question: What are the 6 ELEMENTS of a tourism destination (WTO, 2007)?
flashcards.answer:
1. ATTRACTIONS (natural or cultural; the main pull motive)
2. PUBLIC & PRIVATE AMENITIES (infrastructure + private providers)
3. ACCESSIBILITY (how tourists reach and move around)
4. HUMAN RESOURCES (trained staff + welcoming local community)
5. IMAGE & CHARACTER (awareness + matching expectations)
6. PRICE (costs, exchange rates, profit to reinvest)
flashcards.explanation: Sometimes remembered as the 6 A's: Attractions, Amenities, Access, ... + HR, Image, Price.

flashcards.question: What is DESTINATION MANAGEMENT (WTO, 2007)?
flashcards.answer:
The COORDINATED management of all the elements that make up a destination (attractions, amenities, access, marketing, HR, pricing).

It takes a STRATEGIC approach to link separate entities, avoids duplication (promotion, visitor services, training) and identifies management gaps.
flashcards.explanation: 'Joined-up' coordinated management of all destination elements.

flashcards.question: What is a DMO?
flashcards.answer:
A DESTINATION MANAGEMENT ORGANISATION — the 'manager' of the destination.

It plans the development of the destination, promotes it, and acts as the 'GLUE' between all stakeholders. It uses STRATEGIC PLANNING (long-term planning toward strategic goals, a united vision, consistency of action, quality).
flashcards.explanation: Considers how ENDS (goals) are achieved by MEANS (resources) in a given time.

flashcards.question: What are the 4 STEPS of strategic planning in a destination?
flashcards.answer:
1. SITUATION ANALYSIS — assessing the destination's competitiveness
2. STRATEGIC FRAMEWORK — vision, goals, objectives, core strategies
3. IMPLEMENTATION — turning visions/goals into actions
4. MEASURING effects and performance
flashcards.explanation: Analyse → frame → implement → measure.

flashcards.question: What are the key TASKS of a DMO?
flashcards.answer:
a) Destination PLANNING & development (infrastructure, zoning, environment, product)
b) MARKETING & branding (digital/social, events, partnerships, targeted ads)
c) STAKEHOLDER collaboration & governance
d) SUSTAINABLE tourism practices
e) CRISIS & risk management
flashcards.explanation: Five core task areas of destination management.

flashcards.question: What are the main CHALLENGES in destination management?
flashcards.answer:
• OVERTOURISM — overcrowding, environmental degradation, resident dissatisfaction
• ENVIRONMENTAL concerns — pollution, deforestation, habitat loss
• ECONOMIC DEPENDENCE on tourism — vulnerability to external shocks (need diversification)
• POLITICAL & SOCIAL instability — unrest, terrorism, health crises (e.g. COVID-19)
flashcards.explanation: Four recurring challenges.

flashcards.question: What are the future TRENDS in destination management?
flashcards.answer:
• SMART destinations & digital innovation (big data, AI, AR/VR, contactless)
• REGENERATIVE tourism (leave the destination better than before)
• INCLUSIVE & accessible tourism
• LOCAL & SLOW tourism (quality over quantity, authentic immersive experiences)
flashcards.explanation: Smart, regenerative, inclusive, slow.

learn.title: Destination Management
learn.content:
What Makes a Destination?

6 elements (WTO 2007): Attractions · Amenities (public & private) · Accessibility · Human Resources · Image & Character · Price

Destination Management & the DMO

Coordinated management of all destination elements, taking a strategic approach. The DMO plans, promotes and links stakeholders — the 'glue'.

4 Steps of Strategic Planning

1. Situation analysis → 2. Strategic framework (vision/goals) → 3. Implementation → 4. Measuring performance

DMO Tasks

  • Planning & development · Marketing & branding · Stakeholder governance
  • Sustainable practices · Crisis & risk management

Challenges vs Future Trends

Challenges: overtourism · environment · economic dependence · instability

Trends: smart destinations · regenerative · inclusive/accessible · slow tourism

flashcards.question: What is MASS TOURISM?
flashcards.answer:
A QUANTITATIVE notion based on the proportion of the population participating in tourism or the volume of tourist activity (Burkart & Medlik, 1974).

It means 'extreme concentrations of tourists in one place, resulting in SATURATION'. It can't be tied to fixed numbers — every destination has a different CARRYING CAPACITY.

Origins: Thomas Cook's first organized group tour (1851); developed in Western societies from the 1950s.
flashcards.explanation: Mass tourism = volume + saturation relative to carrying capacity.

flashcards.question: What is FORDISM in tourism?
flashcards.answer:
A stage of 20th-century economic development = the system of MASS PRODUCTION (pioneered by Ford).

In tourism, Fordist systems secure ECONOMIES OF SCALE through large-scale, STANDARDISED and inflexible products — typified by low-cost INCLUSIVE PACKAGE HOLIDAYS from tour operators, who can dominate the distribution chain and depress prices paid to local hotels.
flashcards.explanation: Standardised package holidays = the Fordist model of tourism.

flashcards.question: What are LEAKAGES in tourism?
flashcards.answer:
The part of the price of the holiday paid by tourists that LEAVES or never reaches the destination, due to foreign-based transactions (Mitchell & Page, 2005; Meyer, 2006).

Example: eating at McDonald's, staying at a Hilton, or buying Coke — most of the money goes back to the origin country.
flashcards.explanation: Income that escapes the local economy.

flashcards.question: What is OVERTOURISM?
flashcards.answer:
Term coined by Skift (2016). 'The impact of tourism on a destination that EXCESSIVELY influences the perceived QUALITY OF LIFE of citizens and/or the quality of visitor experiences in a NEGATIVE way.'

It is a new buzzword for existing concepts of tourism CONGESTION MANAGEMENT and CARRYING CAPACITY (UNWTO 2019).
flashcards.explanation: The opposite of Responsible Tourism.

flashcards.question: What is Doxey's IRRIDEX, and what is 'tourismophobia'?
flashcards.answer:
Doxey's IRRITATION INDEX (Irridex, 1975) describes how residents' attitudes EVOLVE over time in response to tourism (from euphoria → apathy → irritation → antagonism).

TOURISMOPHOBIA ('turistofobia', Delgado 2008) describes the antagonistic relationship and escalating tensions between local hosts and incoming tourists (e.g. 'tourists go home' banners; Barcelona after the 1992 Olympics).
flashcards.explanation: Irridex tracks the escalation; tourismophobia is the extreme stage.

flashcards.question: What is CARRYING CAPACITY (UNWTO)?
flashcards.answer: "The maximum number of people that may visit a tourist destination at the same time, without causing destruction of the physical, economic and socio-cultural environment and an unacceptable decrease in the quality of visitors' satisfaction" (UNWTO, 2004).
flashcards.explanation: Key to managing congestion and overtourism.

flashcards.question: What is SPECIAL INTEREST TOURISM (SIT)?
flashcards.answer:
Tourism that occurs when the traveller's MOTIVATION and decision-making are primarily determined by a PARTICULAR SPECIAL INTEREST, with a focus on activity/ies and/or destinations/settings (Hall & Weiler, 1992).

Tourists seek emotional stimuli and experiences ('buy feelings, not products'). Often used as a synonym for NICHE tourism. It reflects the increasing diversity of interests of the late-modern leisure society.
flashcards.explanation: Interest/activity drives the decision — not the destination.

flashcards.question: What is the decision-making difference between GIT, MIT and SIT?
flashcards.answer:
• GIT (General Interest): 'WHERE would I like to go?' — destination first
• MIT (Mixed Interest): 'Where do I want to go AND what activities can I pursue there?'
• SIT (Special Interest): 'WHAT interest/activity do I want to pursue, and WHERE can I do it?' — interest first

For SITs, the destination is no longer primary — the interest/activity is.
flashcards.explanation: The shift from destination-led to interest-led decisions.

flashcards.question: How do General Interest vs Special Interest tourists differ?
flashcards.answer:
GENERAL INTEREST tourist: majority of travellers; lower/lower-middle income; price-sensitive; inexperienced; psychocentric; wants 'fashionable' destinations + high-quality accommodation.

SPECIAL INTEREST tourist: a MINORITY; middle/upper-middle income; LESS price-sensitive; experienced & sophisticated; allocentric/adventurous; high expectations of the activity (not necessarily accommodation); destinations are just contexts for the interest.
flashcards.explanation: Allocentric/experienced (SIT) vs psychocentric/price-sensitive (GIT).

flashcards.question: What are Cohen's 4 TOURIST ROLES (1972)?
flashcards.answer:
1. ORGANIZED MASS TOURIST — all-inclusive tour, 'environmental bubble', max familiarity
2. INDIVIDUAL MASS TOURIST — booked via operator but not bound to a group; slightly more novelty
3. EXPLORER — arranges own travel, avoids 'the beaten track', some familiarity (comfortable base)
4. DRIFTER — max novelty, immersed in local culture, shuns the tourist establishment
flashcards.explanation: From familiarity (mass) to novelty (drifter).

flashcards.question: What are the 4 levels of SIT participant intensity (Brotherton & Himmetoglu, 1997)?
flashcards.answer:
1. BEGINNERS — motivated to pursue a potential interest
2. ENTHUSIASTS — chose a fitting interest, know its boundaries
3. EXPERTS — selected and 'claimed' a special interest; wide knowledge
4. FANATICS — devoted to the field, described by others as 'crazy'
flashcards.explanation: Increasing depth of knowledge, skill and commitment.

learn.title: From Mass & Overtourism to Special Interest Tourism
learn.content:
Mass Tourism

Quantitative notion → volume + saturation vs carrying capacity
Origin: Thomas Cook (1851); boom from the 1950s
Fordism: standardised, inflexible, low-cost package holidays

The Problems

  • Leakages — money that escapes the local economy
  • Overtourism (Skift, 2016) — excessive negative impact on quality of life
  • Doxey's Irridex → 'tourismophobia' (e.g. Barcelona)
  • Carrying capacity — the max visitors without destruction/dissatisfaction

Special Interest Tourism (SIT)

Motivation driven by a particular special interest (≈ niche tourism). Decision logic: GIT 'where?' → MIT 'where + what?' → SIT 'what interest, then where?'

Typologies

Cohen (1972): organized mass → individual mass → explorer → drifter (familiarity → novelty)

Intensity: beginner → enthusiast → expert → fanatic

SIT tourist: minority, less price-sensitive, experienced, allocentric

flashcards.question: What is BUSINESS TOURISM?
flashcards.answer:
A type of tourism activity in which visitors travel for a specific PROFESSIONAL and/or BUSINESS purpose to a place outside their workplace and residence, to attend a meeting, activity or event (UNWTO, 2019).

Key components: MEETINGS, INCENTIVES, CONFERENCES and EXHIBITIONS. It can be combined with other tourism types on the same trip.
flashcards.explanation: Travel for a professional/business purpose.

flashcards.question: What does MICE stand for, and what's the problem with the term?
flashcards.answer:
M = MEETINGS, I = INCENTIVES, C = CONFERENCES (or Congresses), E = EXHIBITIONS (or Events).

PROBLEM: there's no universally agreed definition, and almost no one outside the industry understands it — it's even criticised for its association with rodents/vermin. Alternatives: 'the meetings industry' (introduced 2006), 'business events' (Australia/Canada).
flashcards.explanation: MICE is catchy but poorly understood outside the trade.

flashcards.question: How does the SILK ROUTE relate to business travel history?
flashcards.answer:
In the Middle Ages the Silk Route was perhaps the greatest business travel route of all time. It was important in two ways:
1. It stimulated SUPPORT SYSTEMS for business travellers (accommodation/restaurants — the 'Caravanserai', camel traders, guides).
2. It moved IDEAS and INVENTIONS (gunpowder, astronomy, medicine) between Asia and Europe, and created major trading cities (e.g. Istanbul).
flashcards.explanation: Business travel is ancient — it began with trade.

flashcards.question: What are the main differences between LEISURE and BUSINESS tourism (demand side)?
flashcards.answer:
• WHO PAYS: leisure = the tourist; business = the employer/association (not the traveller)
• WHO DECIDES the destination: leisure = the tourist; business = the meeting/event organizer
• WHEN: leisure = holiday periods & weekends; business = all year, Mon–Fri (July/August avoided)
• DESTINATIONS: leisure = all kinds; business = mostly towns/cities in industrialized countries
flashcards.explanation: Different payer, decider, timing and destinations.

flashcards.question: Why is business tourism BENEFICIAL for destinations?
flashcards.answer:
• Tends to visit in OFF-PEAK season
• Relatively HIGH per-head per-day expenditure
• Business tourists are relatively WELL BEHAVED
• Brings business to many local suppliers (printers, florists, sign-makers…)
• Helps fund infrastructure (e.g. airports) and community leisure facilities
flashcards.explanation: High spend, off-peak, low impact — destinations love it.

flashcards.question: Distinguish CONFERENCE, CONVENTION and CONGRESS.
flashcards.answer:
• CONFERENCE — participatory meeting for discussion/problem-solving; no tradition/periodicity required; usually smaller scale, short duration
• CONVENTION — a general & formal meeting of a body/group to inform, deliberate or set policy; often with a secondary exhibition (US term for large national meetings)
• CONGRESS — regular coming-together of large groups, often several days with simultaneous sessions; (European term for convention)
flashcards.explanation: Scale & formality grow: conference < convention/congress.

flashcards.question: What is INCENTIVE TRAVEL?
flashcards.answer:
A motivational tool: participants receive a TRIP as a REWARD based on specific achievement levels set by management — mostly to increase sales.

Value for the company: bonding, reinforcing corporate culture, loyalty/retention, motivating non-winners. Value for participants: a more memorable prize than cash, networking, professional development, rest, 'trophy value'.
flashcards.explanation: A non-cash reward — often more effective than cash bonuses.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between a B2B and a B2C EXHIBITION?
flashcards.answer:
EXHIBITION = a temporary market event held regularly to showcase a sector and facilitate buying/selling ('shop window').

• TRADE SHOW / B2B — exhibitors from one industry; visitors buy for their business; often invitation/pre-registration; weekday; international/national reach
• CONSUMER SHOW / B2C — open to the public (entrance fee); sells directly to end-users; weekends; local/regional reach

(A 'mixed show' opens to trade then public, e.g. the Paris Air Show.)
flashcards.explanation: B2B = business buyers; B2C = the public.

flashcards.question: What are the ICCA vs UIA criteria for an international association meeting?
flashcards.answer:
ICCA (International Congress & Convention Association): organized by an international/regional association HQ; 50+ participants; held REGULARLY; rotates between at least 3 countries.

UIA (Union of International Associations): minimum 300 participants; lasting at least 3 days; representatives from at least 5 countries.
flashcards.explanation: ICCA = 50+/3 countries; UIA = 300+/3 days/5 countries.

learn.title: Business Tourism (MICE)
learn.content:
What is Business Tourism?

Travel for a professional/business purpose to attend an event.
MICE = Meetings · Incentives · Conferences · Exhibitions

Also called 'the meetings industry' (2006) or 'business events' — MICE is catchy but poorly understood outside the trade. Business travel is ancient (the Silk Route + Caravanserai).

Leisure vs Business (demand side)

Who pays? Employer/association · Who decides? The organizer · When? All year, Mon–Fri · Where? Cities in industrialized countries

Why Destinations Want It

Off-peak · high per-head spend · well-behaved · supports many local suppliers · funds infrastructure.

Key Formats

Conference < Convention/Congress (scale & formality)

Incentive travel — a trip as a reward (often beats cash)

Exhibitions: B2B (trade, weekday, invite) vs B2C (public, weekend, fee)

ICCA 50+/3 countries · UIA 300+/3 days/5 countries

flashcards.question: What is CULTURAL TOURISM (UNWTO, 2019)?
flashcards.answer:
A type of tourism where the visitor's essential motivation is to LEARN, DISCOVER, EXPERIENCE and CONSUME the tangible and intangible cultural attractions/products of a destination.

These relate to a society's material, intellectual, spiritual and emotional features: arts & architecture, historical/cultural heritage, culinary heritage, literature, music, creative industries and living cultures.
flashcards.explanation: Motivation = to learn/experience culture.

flashcards.question: What are the 3 areas included in cultural tourism (UNWTO, 2018)?
flashcards.answer:
1. TANGIBLE heritage — national/world heritage sites, monuments, historic buildings, cultural routes
2. INTANGIBLE heritage — crafts, gastronomy, festivals, music, oral traditions, religious/spiritual
3. CONTEMPORARY culture — film, performing arts, design, fashion, new media
flashcards.explanation: Tangible + intangible + contemporary.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between HERITAGE and HISTORY (and arts tourism)?
flashcards.answer:
HISTORY = the past itself.
HERITAGE = the modern-day USE and VALUATION of the past (for tourism, education, etc.) — 'what we inherit from the past and value in the present'.

Cultural tourism covers both HERITAGE tourism (artefacts of the past) and ARTS tourism (contemporary cultural production).
flashcards.explanation: Heritage = the present use of the past.

flashcards.question: What are McKercher's 5 TYPES of cultural tourist (2002)?
flashcards.answer:
Based on two dimensions — CENTRALITY (how important culture is to the trip) and DEPTH of experience:
1. PURPOSEFUL (high centrality / deep)
2. SIGHTSEEING (high centrality / shallow)
3. CASUAL (modest centrality / shallow)
4. INCIDENTAL (low centrality / shallow)
5. SERENDIPITOUS (low centrality / deep)
flashcards.explanation: Centrality × depth = 5 cultural-tourist types.

flashcards.question: What is the VALUE of tourism for culture, and of culture for tourism?
flashcards.answer:
VALUE OF TOURISM FOR CULTURE: generates resources for conservation, motivates communities to manage cultural assets, raises awareness of local heritage.

VALUE OF CULTURE FOR TOURISM: gives coherence to the destination offer, increases competitiveness, increases length of stay, spending and satisfaction.
flashcards.explanation: A two-way value relationship.

flashcards.question: What are the main TYPES of heritage attraction (Timothy, 2021)?
flashcards.answer:
• MUSEUMS (local, art, science, sports, music)
• HISTORIC THEME PARKS / folk-life museums (living museums, e.g. Plimoth Plantation)
• PERFORMING ARTS (opera houses, theatres — building + performance)
• ARCHAEOLOGICAL SITES & ancient monuments (Stonehenge, Pyramids, Acropolis)
• RELIGIOUS sites · LIVING culture / ethnic tourism · LITERARY & FILM locations
• AGRITOURISM & food tourism · SITES OF DEATH (dark tourism) · HERITAGE FESTIVALS
flashcards.explanation: A wide range — from museums to dark-tourism sites.

flashcards.question: What is the role of pilgrimage and the GRAND TOUR in heritage tourism history?
flashcards.answer:
PILGRIMAGE — one of the EARLIEST forms of heritage tourism: travel for spiritual/religious experiences to burial sites, miracle sites, healing places.

The GRAND TOUR (1600s–mid 1800s) — young European men of means travelled (with tutors) to classical art cities of Italy, France, etc. to become 'cultured nobility' — among the earliest prepackaged cultural tours.
flashcards.explanation: Pilgrimage + Grand Tour = historical roots of cultural tourism.

learn.title: Cultural Tourism
learn.content:
Definition

Motivation = to learn, discover, experience and consume a destination's tangible & intangible cultural attractions (UNWTO, 2019).

Three Areas (UNWTO 2018)

  • Tangible — monuments, heritage sites, historic buildings
  • Intangible — crafts, gastronomy, festivals, music, oral/spiritual
  • Contemporary — film, performing arts, design, fashion, new media

Heritage vs History

History = the past. Heritage = the present-day use and valuation of the past. Cultural tourism = heritage tourism + arts tourism.

McKercher's 5 Cultural Tourists (centrality × depth)

Purposeful · Sightseeing · Casual · Incidental · Serendipitous

Heritage Attractions & History

Museums · living museums · performing arts · archaeological sites · religious sites · living culture · literary/film locations · agritourism · dark-tourism sites · festivals

Roots: pilgrimage (earliest) and the Grand Tour (1600s–1800s)

flashcards.question: What is INDUSTRIAL TOURISM?
flashcards.answer:
A form of tourism that involves visits to modern WORK FACILITIES to view products and services, the PROCESS by which they are created, and the PEOPLE involved (Robinson, in Jafari 2003).

It is generally considered a form of CULTURAL TOURISM. Visits can be guided tours, observation from galleries, or purpose-built visitor centres (factories, mines, power plants, wineries, theatres).
flashcards.explanation: Visiting workplaces to see how things are made.

flashcards.question: What are the 2 TYPES of industrial tourism?
flashcards.answer:
1. ACTIVE industrial tourism — visits to WORKING companies/organisations, to learn about PRODUCTION PROCESSES in real time.

2. INDUSTRIAL HERITAGE tourism (industrial archaeology) — visits to INACTIVE / abandoned industrial sites, to learn about PAST industrial knowledge, culture and identity.
flashcards.explanation: Working sites (active) vs abandoned sites (heritage).

flashcards.question: What roles does industrial tourism play in ORGANISATIONS?
flashcards.answer:
• PUBLIC RELATIONS — building relations with the local community, employees, partners, media; improving reputation & corporate social responsibility; demonstrating 'green'/sustainable operations
• MARKETING — strengthening BRAND ATTACHMENT and encouraging purchases; factory tours & corporate museums as 'events & experiences' (Kotler & Keller)
flashcards.explanation: Two key business functions: PR and marketing.

flashcards.question: How does industrial tourism connect to the EXPERIENCE ECONOMY?
flashcards.answer:
In the experience economy, the economic value of an offering INCREASES from raw material → product → service → EXPERIENCE (Pine & Gilmore, 1998).

Experiences are built on four dimensions: ENTERTAINMENT, EDUCATIONAL, ESCAPIST and AESTHETIC. Industrial tourism turns work into a memorable, multi-sensory experience — and experiences are the foundation of special interest tourism.
flashcards.explanation: Work becomes a paid, memorable experience.

flashcards.question: What is the historical origin of industrial tourism?
flashcards.answer:
The first factory tours took place in GREAT BRITAIN in the 18th century. There is evidence tourists visited companies over 150 years ago — French vineyards & chocolate factories, US whiskey distilleries, tobacco factories, mines and stock exchanges.

MacCannell describes it as putting WORK ON DISPLAY — 'musealising' work and making it a tourist attraction.
flashcards.explanation: 18th-century Britain; 'work on display'.

flashcards.question: What does INDUSTRIAL HERITAGE protect, and why revitalise it?
flashcards.answer:
Industrial heritage = remains of TEXTILE, MINING, STEEL and similar heavy industries (TICCIH protects buildings, machinery, mills, mines, warehouses, power plants, transport, workers' social spaces).

Revitalising former industrial areas for tourism brings ECONOMIC (new jobs/income), SOCIAL (resident engagement) and CULTURAL (new identity, slowing depopulation) benefits — a sustainable way to divert crowds from saturated areas.
flashcards.explanation: Reusing the industrial past for regional renewal.

learn.title: Industrial Tourism
learn.content:
Definition

Visits to work facilities to see products, the production process, and the people involved — generally a form of cultural tourism.

Two Types

Active — working companies, learn the production process in real time

Industrial heritage — abandoned/inactive sites (mines, mills), learn the past

Roles in Organisations

  • Public relations — reputation, community/employee/media relations, 'green' image
  • Marketing — brand attachment, encouraging purchases (factory tours, corporate museums)

Experience Economy

Value rises: raw material → product → service → experience (Pine & Gilmore). Four dimensions: entertainment, educational, escapist, aesthetic. Experiences are the foundation of special interest tourism.

History & Heritage

First factory tours: 18th-century Britain; 'work on display' (MacCannell). Industrial heritage (textile/mining/steel; protected by TICCIH) revitalises regions — economic, social & cultural renewal.
